claims.text: Elevated-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coatings is governed by dynamic microstructural evolution.
Oxide-layer formation and growth are key components of the microstructural evolution governing wear resistance.
Redistribution of alloying elements is a key component of the microstructural evolution governing wear resistance.
Oxide-layer evolution and alloying-element redistribution during wear can be directly observed by in-situ TEM or X-ray CT.
Temperature and loading conditions influence the dynamic microstructural evolution of the coating during wear.
Wear resistance will improve as temperature increases, up to a critical temperature.
Formation of a protective oxide layer causes the predicted improvement in wear resistance.
An optimized distribution of alloying elements contributes to the predicted improvement in wear resistance.
The proposed hypothesis applies over a temperature range of 20°C to 800°C.
The proposed hypothesis applies to sliding or abrasive wear under moderate to high contact pressures.
Beyond an uncertain combination of temperature and load, oxide formation and alloying-element redistribution may become detrimental to wear resistance.
Failure to observe a significant correlation between microstructural evolution and wear resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe improved wear resistance with increasing temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
